text.p: Pharmaceuticals and chemicals company Zeneca Group Plc on Thursday hailed a strong improvement in its first-half profit margins, which it said resulted from restructuring, a better mix of products and the transfer of some launch costs to the second half.

Currency hedging had helped to protect the group's overseas earnings against the worst excesses of the strong pound. But sterling strength had still reduced sales by 300 million stg and operating profits by a little over 90 million stg, chief executive Sir David Barnes said in a telephone interview with Reuters
He said he expected a similar negative impact in the second half if foreign exchange rates stayed at current levels.
Barnes described the results as "cracking good".

"Most pleasing to me is the improvement in the margin we have had from 21.2 percent to 24 percent in the first half and that is after soaking up the adverse currency hit. That is a very good set of figures and improvements have come across all three sectors -- pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals and specialities," he said

Barnes said the gain was a result of restructuring undertaken last year, notably reorganisation of the seeds business and disposal of textile colours, and an improvement in the mix of products, with higher margin new products being rolled out.
The third factor was the shifting of some launch costs anticipated in the first half of the year to the second half.

"There will be substantial new product launch costs to come in the second half of the year," said Barnes, who predicted that full-year margins would be two to 2.5 percentage points lower than the half year figure, in line with the group's historic performance.
Among individual products, Barnes said cardiovascular drug Zestril had increased market share in the U.S. to 19.9 percent at the end of the second quarter from 19.5 percent at the start of the year.
He said this was partly a result of new indications, such as use following heart attacks, and the preference for using ACE inhibitors in patients who were diabetic.

Barnes said he did not believe the recent flurry over new asthma pill Accolate, which led to the company changing the drug's label in the U.S. after it was linked to six cases of the rare asthma-related Churg-Strauss Syndrome, would damage the product.
Sales of Accolate in the first half totalled 19 million stg, with 300,000 patients now using the drug. Barnes said the product had already gained eight percent of the asthma controller market.
He said the reported cases of Churg-Strauss, of which only three were definite, were linked to people who "received such great benefit from Accolate that they started to reduce their oral steroids."

"One of the great things with Accolate is that we have had more spontaneous expressions and anecdotal reports of patients receiving great relief than with any other product we have ever launched," Barnes added.
Barnes said the group's new migraine drug Zomig, acquired from Glaxo Wellcome Plc, had been well received by doctors and patients in its first few weeks of launch in Britain.
The company is to update analysts and investors on the 45 products in its product pipeline at presentations in Britain and the U.S. on December 1 and 2.

The group hopes this will counter criticism that it faces a gap in its product portfolio in the medium term, which some analysts say will become more noticeable when its top-selling drug Zestril loses patent protection on December 31, 2001.

"The products we have recently launched - Casodex, Merrem, Zoladex, Zomig, Accolate and now potentially Seroquel - will be growing strongly in five years time when we face the patent expiry for Zestril," Barnes said.
"We will see a slower rate of growth in 2002 if we don't do anything about it, but we are talking about a slower rate of growth not a decline," he added.
